answer.rationale: The write-path p99 is 5x target during settlement peak, but the new release cannot be rolled back, so rollback_release is ruled out by compliance. Regional failover is proven fast, but it is a large blast-radius move while writes are at peak, and it does not directly reduce write-path load; it also risks write disruption during heavy settlement traffic, so I would reserve it only if latency keeps worsening after the smaller action. Add capacity is plausible, but provisioning headroom before retail peak is the pattern I remember, and adding capacity now may not be fast enough or targeted enough for the immediate p99 climb. Circuit breakers are useful for containing a dependency outage, but there is no evidence here that an external payments partner is failing; enabling one could shed writes and therefore conflicts with the objective of preserving customer writes. Routing report/dashboard/read queries to replicas was validated in memory_b5, where it removed load from the primary and allowed transactional write latency to recover the same day. Since the current bottleneck is write-path latency at peak settlement traffic, shifting non-transactional read/report load off the primary is the most direct, least destructive way to recover write headroom without losing customer writes. I would verify memory_b5 first because the intervention's success depends on there being meaningful read/report load on the primary; if the source record shows the effect was larger or more directly causal than the consolidated memory implies, I proceed; if not, I may still proceed but with tighter monitoring and a fallback to add_capacity/regional_failover.
